blocks.text: A forged gear is heated until it is austenitic and then plunged into oil. If it cools too slowly the teeth turn into soft pearlite; if it is quenched fast enough they become hard martensite, but a thick hub may still cool too slowly in its centre. Predicting which microstructure forms at each point is done with time-temperature-transformation diagrams, which are simply maps of how fast austenite decomposes at each temperature.

blocks.markdown: Above the eutectoid temperature $A_1$ (727 C for plain carbon steel) austenite is stable. Below $A_1$ it is unstable and decomposes, but the *rate* depends strongly on temperature. Just below $A_1$ there is a small driving force, so transformation is slow (a few hundred seconds); at lower temperature the driving force is large but diffusion becomes slower. The product, and the speed of the reaction, depend on the balance of these two effects, producing a C-shaped curve with a fastest point, the **nose**.

blocks.title: TTT diagram
blocks.text: A **time-temperature-transformation (TTT) diagram**, also called an isothermal transformation diagram, shows the time needed for austenite to start and to finish transforming when a sample is cooled very quickly to a fixed temperature and held there. Temperature is on the vertical axis and time (logarithmic) on the horizontal axis. Each curve is a C shape, with the start of transformation at the left and the finish at the right.

blocks.caption: Illustrative isothermal transformation data for a eutectoid (about 0.8 wt% C) plain carbon steel, with Ms about 220 C. Real values depend on composition and grain size.

blocks.markdown: **Reading the products.** Above the nose, diffusion is fast and austenite transforms to **pearlite**, a lamellar mixture of ferrite and cementite: coarse pearlite (soft) at higher temperatures, fine pearlite (harder) near the nose. Below the nose, the product is **bainite**, a fine, non-lamellar mixture of ferrite and cementite that forms by a partly diffusive mechanism; upper bainite (feathery) forms at higher temperature and lower bainite (needle-like, tougher and harder) at lower temperature. Below the **martensite start temperature** $M_s$ (about 220 C for a eutectoid steel, typical) austenite transforms by a diffusionless shear to **martensite**, very hard and brittle. Martensite formation is **athermal**: the amount depends on how far the temperature falls below $M_s$, not on the time spent at that temperature.

blocks.caption: Koistinen-Marburger relation: f_M is the fraction of austenite transformed to martensite on cooling to temperature T (in C), M_s the martensite start temperature, and 0.011 per K a typical constant for plain carbon steels.

blocks.title: Reading microstructures from a TTT diagram
blocks.prompt: Using the table, predict the microstructure after (a) quenching to 600 C and holding 100 s, then quenching to room temperature, and (b) quenching directly to room temperature. For (b) estimate the fraction of martensite at 100 C using $M_s=220$ C.

steps.text: Path (a): at 600 C, transformation starts at 3 s and finishes at 30 s, so by 100 s the austenite has fully transformed to fine pearlite, and the later quench changes nothing.
Path (b): the quench is faster than the nose, so no pearlite or bainite forms; austenite survives to $M_s$ and then transforms to martensite as the temperature falls. At 100 C the fraction is
At 20 C the relation gives $f_M=0.89$, so about 11 % retained austenite remains with the martensite; the structure is mostly martensite.

blocks.answer: (a) 100 % fine pearlite, soft; (b) mostly martensite (73 % at 100 C, about 89 % at room temperature, the rest retained austenite), very hard.

blocks.markdown: **Critical cooling rate.** To form martensite, the cooling curve must pass to the left of the nose so that pearlite and bainite do not start. The slowest cooling that just misses the nose is the **critical cooling rate**. On an isothermal diagram it can be estimated as the straight line from $A_1$ to the nose, and that line's slope is the critical rate. Alloying elements (Cr, Mo, Mn, Ni) delay pearlite and bainite formation, moving the nose to longer times and lowering the critical cooling rate, so thick sections can be hardened (higher hardenability).

blocks.caption: A1 is the eutectoid temperature, T_nose and t_nose the temperature and time at the nose of the transformation start curve.

blocks.title: Critical cooling rate for a plain carbon eutectoid steel
blocks.prompt: A eutectoid steel has $A_1=727$ C and its isothermal transformation start curve has its nose at 550 C and 1 s. Estimate the critical cooling rate for martensite. What happens in a section that cools at 60 C/s?

steps.text: Temperature drop from $A_1$ to the nose.
Divide by the time at the nose.
A section cooling at only 60 C/s is below the critical rate, so its cooling curve cuts the pearlite start curve: pearlite (and possibly bainite) forms and the section will not harden fully.

blocks.answer: About 177 C/s from the isothermal diagram (about 140 C/s from a continuous cooling diagram, see below); a 60 C/s section would contain pearlite.

blocks.markdown: **CCT diagrams.** Real heat treatments cool continuously, not isothermally. A **continuous-cooling transformation (CCT)** diagram plots the start and finish of transformation along cooling curves. Compared with the TTT diagram of the same steel, the CCT curves are displaced to **longer times and lower temperatures**, because the steel spends less time at each temperature on the way down. For a plain eutectoid steel, continuous cooling gives no bainite: the cooling curves either cross the pearlite region or miss it and form martensite. The critical cooling rate from the CCT diagram is therefore lower than that estimated from the TTT nose (140 rather than 177 C/s for the example above, typical).

blocks.title: How to use the diagrams
blocks.text: Draw the actual cooling path over the diagram. Cross a transformation start curve and the product that curve represents begins to form; stay to the left of the nose all the way to $M_s$ and martensite forms. If the path crosses the curves, the structure is a mixture of the products formed in each region, plus martensite from the austenite remaining when $M_s$ is reached.

blocks.title: Section size and surface-versus-centre cooling
blocks.text: The surface of a quenched part cools much faster than its core. A TTT or CCT diagram applies to a single cooling path, so for a thick section the surface may become martensite and the core pearlite or bainite. Alloying steels (higher hardenability) are used for thick sections because they move the nose to the right.

points: A TTT diagram gives the time for austenite to start and finish transforming at constant temperature; above the nose the product is pearlite, below it bainite, and below Ms martensite, which forms athermally ($f_M=1-\exp[-0.011(M_s-T)]$).
The critical cooling rate to avoid pearlite is approximated by $(A_1-T_{\text{nose}})/t_{\text{nose}}$; alloying shifts the nose to the right and lowers it.
CCT diagrams describe continuous cooling and are displaced to longer times and lower temperatures than TTT diagrams; plain eutectoid steel shows no bainite on continuous cooling.

questions.stem: What is the essential difference between a TTT diagram and a CCT diagram of the same steel?

options.text: TTT describes only martensite and CCT describes only pearlite
TTT is plotted against cooling rate, whereas CCT is plotted against composition
TTT describes transformation at a constant hold temperature, whereas CCT describes transformation during continuous cooling
They are identical, but the CCT diagram has a linear time axis

questions.correctOptionText: TTT describes transformation at a constant hold temperature, whereas CCT describes transformation during continuous cooling

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: both diagrams show the pearlite, bainite and martensite regions.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: both use temperature against log time; composition is not an axis.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: TTT data come from isothermal holds and CCT data from continuous cooling paths.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: both use a logarithmic time axis, and the curves differ in position, not in the axis.

questions.explanation: To obtain a TTT diagram the sample is cooled quickly to a given temperature and held, while for a CCT diagram it is cooled at a controlled rate. Because the steel spends time at higher temperatures on the way down, the CCT curves are displaced to longer times and lower temperatures.

questions.stem: Using the illustrative data for a eutectoid steel (fine pearlite at 600 C starts at 3 s and finishes at 30 s), what microstructure results from quenching to 600 C, holding 100 s, and then quenching to room temperature?

options.text: Fine pearlite, fully transformed
Martensite
A mixture of bainite and martensite
Untransformed austenite

distractorRationale.a: Correct: 100 s exceeds the 30 s finish time, so the transformation is complete.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: martensite forms only from austenite that survives to Ms, and none remains.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: no bainite forms at 600 C, which is above the nose.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: austenite is unstable at 600 C and has fully decomposed.

questions.explanation: Transformation at 600 C starts after 3 s and finishes after 30 s, so a 100 s hold is long enough to transform all the austenite to fine pearlite. The subsequent quench cannot alter this structure.

questions.stem: A eutectoid steel has a martensite start temperature of 220 C and the bainite start time at 250 C is 60 s. It is quenched to 250 C, held for 10 s and then quenched to room temperature. What microstructure is obtained?

options.text: Fully bainitic, because 250 C is in the bainite range
Fine pearlite, because the steel was cooled slowly
Untransformed austenite, because martensite cannot form from austenite
Mostly martensite, because no bainite has formed in 10 s and the austenite transforms on cooling below Ms

questions.correctOptionText: Mostly martensite, because no bainite has formed in 10 s and the austenite transforms on cooling below Ms

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: bainite needs at least 60 s at that temperature, and the hold is too short.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: the quench to 250 C was rapid, so pearlite did not form.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: martensite forms from austenite below Ms by a diffusionless shear.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: 10 s is shorter than the 60 s needed for bainite to start, so the austenite is intact when cooling passes Ms.

questions.explanation: Reading the diagram at 250 C, the bainite start time is 60 s, so a 10 s hold leaves the austenite untransformed. On cooling below $M_s=220$ C it converts to martensite, with perhaps a little retained austenite.

questions.stem: Which statement describes the critical cooling rate for martensite formation in a steel?

options.text: It is the fastest cooling rate that can be achieved in water and is unaffected by composition
It is the slowest cooling rate whose path just misses the nose of the transformation start curve, and it is lowered by alloying elements such as Cr and Mo
It is the cooling rate needed to reach room temperature within one hour
It is the rate at which martensite begins to decompose

questions.correctOptionText: It is the slowest cooling rate whose path just misses the nose of the transformation start curve, and it is lowered by alloying elements such as Cr and Mo

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: it is a property of the steel, not of the quenchant.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: it is the tangent to the nose, and elements that delay pearlite and bainite shift the nose right and reduce the rate required.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: the rate refers to the high-temperature range through the nose, not to room temperature.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: this describes tempering, not the critical cooling rate.

questions.explanation: If the cooling curve passes to the left of the nose, neither pearlite nor bainite starts, and martensite forms at Ms. Alloying elements move the nose to the right, so slower cooling suffices, which is what is meant by higher hardenability.

questions.stem: A plain carbon eutectoid steel is cooled continuously at 120 C/s from 727 C to room temperature. Its isothermal diagram has the nose at 550 C and 1 s, whereas its continuous cooling diagram has a critical cooling rate of 140 C/s. Which result is correct?

options.text: The cooling is faster than the CCT critical rate, so the structure is fully martensitic
The steel forms only bainite, because the rate is moderate
No transformation occurs at any cooling rate
The cooling is slower than the CCT critical rate, so some pearlite forms before martensite

questions.correctOptionText: The cooling is slower than the CCT critical rate, so some pearlite forms before martensite

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: the rate is lower than the critical value, not higher.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: a plain eutectoid steel shows no bainite on continuous cooling.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: the steel transforms at any cooling rate; the product changes.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: 120 C/s is below the critical rate of 140 C/s, so the cooling curve crosses the pearlite start curve.

questions.explanation: The critical rate from the CCT diagram is the appropriate one for continuous cooling, and 120 C/s lies below it, so the cooling curve intersects the pearlite start curve. A mixture of pearlite and martensite results, and the steel does not harden fully. Using the isothermal estimate of 177 C/s would have led to the same conclusion here.

questions.stem: A different steel has an isothermal bainite reaction at 400 C that starts at 4 s, is 50 % complete at 40 s and finishes at 400 s. The steel is quenched to 400 C, held for 40 s and then quenched to room temperature, where all the remaining austenite transforms to martensite. What percentage of the final microstructure is martensite?
questions.explanation: At the 50 % point of the bainite curve, half of the austenite has become bainite and the other half remains austenite. On the final quench this remainder converts to martensite, so the final structure is about 50 % bainite and 50 % martensite.

questions.stem: A steel with $A_1=725$ C has the nose of its isothermal start curve at 500 C and 20 s. Estimate the critical cooling rate for avoiding pearlite and bainite, using $(A_1-T_{\text{nose}})/t_{\text{nose}}$, in C per second.
questions.explanation: The temperature interval from $A_1$ to the nose is $725-500=225$ C, and the time at the nose is 20 s. The estimated critical cooling rate is $225/20=11.25$ C/s, much lower than for the plain carbon steel because the alloying elements delay the transformation.

questions.stem: A steel has $M_s=300$ C and the Koistinen-Marburger relation $f_M=1-\exp[-0.011(M_s-T)]$ applies, with temperatures in C. What fraction of austenite is martensite on cooling to 150 C? Give a value between 0 and 1.
questions.explanation: The undercooling below $M_s$ is $300-150=150$ C, so $0.011\times150=1.65$. Then $f_M=1-\exp(-1.65)=1-0.192=0.808$, so about 81 % of the austenite has become martensite and the remainder is retained austenite.

questions.stem: A eutectoid steel is quenched from the austenite region along three different paths. Using the typical isothermal data (fine pearlite at 600 C finishes at 30 s; lower bainite at 350 C starts at 10 s, is 50 % complete at 100 s and finishes at 1000 s; Ms about 220 C), predict the microstructure for each path: (a) quench to 600 C and hold 1 h, (b) quench to 350 C and hold 2000 s, (c) quench directly to 20 C. Say which is hardest and why.
markingGuide: (a) Fine pearlite: the hold far exceeds the 30 s finish time at 600 C
(b) Lower bainite: transformation finishes at 1000 s so 2000 s is complete
(c) Martensite, with some retained austenite: no pearlite or bainite forms if the cooling is faster than the critical rate
Martensite is the hardest: supersaturated carbon in a distorted body-centred tetragonal lattice with a high dislocation density, forming by a diffusionless shear
Order of hardness: martensite > lower bainite > fine pearlite
States that martensite is brittle and usually tempered
questions.explanation: Each path stays in a different region of the diagram, so the product follows directly from the temperature and hold time. Martensite is the hardest because carbon cannot diffuse out and the lattice is highly strained.

questions.stem: Explain how the critical cooling rate for martensite is found from a TTT diagram, how alloying elements change it, and why a continuous-cooling transformation diagram should be used instead for real quenching. A 40 mm round bar of a steel with a critical cooling rate of 60 C/s is quenched in oil; its surface cools at 150 C/s and its centre at 20 C/s through the pearlite range. Describe the resulting microstructure.
markingGuide: Critical cooling rate: slope of the line from A1 to the nose of the start curve, $(A_1-T_{\text{nose}})/t_{\text{nose}}$
Alloying elements (Cr, Mo, Mn, Ni) move the nose to longer times, lowering the critical rate and increasing hardenability
TTT is for isothermal holds; real quenching is continuous, so the transformation occurs later and at lower temperature, and CCT curves should be used (a slightly lower critical rate)
Surface cooling at 150 C/s exceeds 60 C/s, so the surface is martensitic
The centre cooling at 20 C/s is below 60 C/s, so the centre transforms to pearlite or bainite and is softer
Conclusion: hardness decreases from the surface to the centre; a more hardenable (alloyed) steel or faster quenchant would give deeper hardening
questions.explanation: The nose marks where transformation is fastest, so the cooling path must pass to the left of it to form martensite. In the thick bar, the surface exceeds the critical rate while the centre does not, so the microstructure and hardness vary through the section.
